source.title: A random matrix analysis of random Fourier features: beyond the Gaussian kernel, a precise phase transition, and the corresponding double descent
source.authors: Zhenyu Liao; Romain Couillet; Michael W. Mahoney

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests double descent in random Fourier feature regression, a different model class from the deep-network settings in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-error sweeps over feature count and regularization, which bear on V4, and a regularization setting that bears on part of V6. It does not sweep training epochs or training-sample count. Values for the test-error curves are reported in figures rather than as numerical tables.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps the number of random Fourier features on MNIST-like data and measures test MSE, as in the RFF experiments of Belkin et al. (arXiv:1812.11118). It also sweeps ridge λ, which bears on V4 and on V6's regularization part. It additionally derives the curve theoretically, but the empirical sweeps essentially replicate the original RFF setting with ridge regression rather than min-norm interpolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors derive exact large n, p, N asymptotics for RFF ridge regression with only mild data assumptions. They identify an under- to over-parameterization phase transition at 2N = n and derive the resulting double-descent test curve (a singular peak as λ→0). Theory matches real-data experiments, and larger or tuned ridge smooths the peak away.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random Fourier feature ridge regression with cosine and sine features, rather than the original deep-network or broader model settings; varies feature count and regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: The test-error curve depends on regularization: small λ values show double descent, while larger λ values yield smoother, monotonically decreasing curves. The authors also report dataset-specific experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: The correction parameters (δcos, δsin) and γ jump sharply at 2N = n for small λ; the jump is smoothed for large λ (Figs 6, 8, 12). The authors argue double descent is a consequence of this under/over-parameterized phase transition (Remark 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent in random-feature models is the test-error manifestation of a sharp under- to over-parameterization phase transition in the resolvent, located at 2N = n.

record.problems: Empirical curve results are primarily graphical rather than tabulated numerically. The reported sweeps cover specific datasets and feature-regression settings, not deep networks; no uncertainty intervals or error bars are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying test-error results omitted.

untested.parts: No deep networks; RFF is only a single random hidden layer with fixed weights.
No sweep over training time; closed-form ridge solution.
n is fixed in the test-error sweeps; no sample-count sweep.
Only RFF ridge regression on binary MNIST-type tasks; other model classes are not tested.
No single complexity measure is tested across axes. The peak location 2N = n is shown only along the feature axis.
Label noise or variance as the driver, and multiple or split peaks, are not tested.

missing.what: Theoretical result: in the ridgeless limit, Ω diverges at 2N = n, so asymptotic test MSE → ∞ while training MSE stays zero. This proves the singular peak for generic data.
missing.locator: Section 4.1 (Asymptotic test MSE as λ→0); Lemma 5; Section 1.2 contribution 2

missing.what: For any fixed λ > 0, minimum test error lies in the over-parameterized 2N > n regime. The global optimum is a highly over-parameterized model with non-vanishing λ.
The peak disappears when test data are close perturbations of training data (noise variance σ² < λ), so peak existence depends on train-test dissimilarity.

record.verdict_notes: Belkin et al. (an original source) also used RFF on MNIST, hence T1 for V4. This study, however, uses ridge regression with tiny λ rather than min-norm interpolation, and binary subsets with n = 500. All test-curve evidence is figure-only, with no error bars; results are averaged over 30 runs. The peak sits at 2N = n because RFF has 2N features (cos and sin).

versions.untested_parts: The study uses random Fourier features, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No sweep over the number of training samples near the interpolation threshold.
Tests feature-count curves for random Fourier feature regression on the reported datasets; does not establish the curve across all model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across model size, epochs, and sample count.
Tests the regularization-related claim that a tuned penalty removes the singular peak. Label noise or variance as a cause, and multiple or split peaks, are not tested.
Does not compare the curve with an effective parameter count or test whether that recasting makes it an ordinary U-shaped curve.
